extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato, classics, and political/philosophical theory
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidelines from Plato's Republic (Book 3) for what may be taught, shown, and practised in the education of the guardian class — covering poetry/myth, music, rhythm, instruments, visual arts, gymnastic training, diet, and moral exemplars. Intended as prescriptive rules for shaping character and public culture in the ideal city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of representing gods or worthy men overcome by laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians, and the poetry permitted in the State, must not represent persons of worth — and especially the gods — as overcome by laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example cited: Homer’s line about 'Inextinguishable laughter arose among the blessed gods' is unacceptable. Laughter that is indulged to excess produces violent reaction; portrayals that make gods or guardians appear ridiculous are disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness prized; lying allowed only to rulers for the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is to be highly valued; lying is regarded as useless to the gods and only as a medicine for men, and if lying is permitted at all it must be restricted to rulers acting for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private individuals must not lie (and lying to rulers is a grave fault). If a ruler catches any non-ruler lying, that person will be punished as introducing a subversive practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Youth must be trained to temperance (obedience and self-control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief elements of temperance: obedience to commanders and self-control in sensual pleasures; youths must be brought up to conform to these virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language, poetry, and examples that promote impertinence to rulers, drunkenness, or sensual excess (quoted Homeric taunts and paeans to feasting/drinking) are to be excluded because they do not conduce to temperance and may harm young men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid praise or modelling of love of gifts and money
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems or stories that praise bribery, gifts persuading gods/kings, or that represent heroes as motivated by money or gifts must be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific anti-examples: Phoenix advising Achilles to accept gifts; portrayals of Achilles as avaricious or restoring Hector only for payment are not to be approved or repeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude tales where gods or heroes commit immoral or impious acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets must not represent gods or demigods as authors of evil or portray heroes/sons of gods committing heinous acts (e.g., rape, impiety); such tales should be either denied or revised so as not to attribute evil to divine figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either the poet must assert the acts were not done by those figures or deny their divine parentage. Rationale: allowing such tales engenders laxity of morals by giving license to excuse vice as 'like the gods.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit imitation (mimesis) in the education of guardians to virtuous characters
rubrics_metrics.description: If guardians imitate (act/perform), they should only personate characters that are suitable to their profession: courageous, temperate, holy, free, etc.; they must not practice imitating base, unmanly, or vicious characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibited impersonations include: women quarrelling, persons in sickness, love, or labour, slaves performing slave-offices, mad or bad people, or any behaviour that would form bad habits. Imitation from early youth becomes second nature — hence the restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pantomimic/pervasive imitation (imitating all sounds/roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pantomimic style — performers who imitate every sound or role (animals, thunder, instruments) and adopt many characters — is unsuitable for guardians and should be excluded from the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of pantomime: barking like a dog, bleating like a sheep, imitating thunder, creaking wheels, or imitating musical instruments. Such exhaustive imitation encourages vice and instability of character in guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple narrative or restrained imitation style only (imitator of virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two basic styles identified: (1) simple narration with little imitation, and (2) imitative/pantomimic. The Republic prefers either the simple style or a pure imitator of virtue — i.e., the style that predominantly presents virtuous action — and rejects mixed/pantomimic styles for guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mixed (epic) style is charming but the mixed/pantomimic is popular with children and common people; in the ideal State the guardians must not be trained in manifold imitation but in one consistent mode that models virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban musical modes/harmonies expressive of sorrow, softness, or drunkenness
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain harmonies (e.g., mixed/tenor Lydian, full-toned/bass Lydian, Ionian) are associated with sorrow, softness, or drunkenness and are unsuitable for guardians and even for decent women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'relaxed' modes are useless or harmful for guardians. They are explicitly to be banished; instead one should retain modes expressive of courage and temperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain only Dorian and Phrygian harmonies for songs of guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep harmonies that express the 'strain of necessity' and the 'strain of freedom' — the tones appropriate for courage and temperance — identified as the Dorian and Phrygian modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two harmonies are to supply the musical vocabulary for crises (courage under danger) and for peace/temperate behaviour. They replace multiplicity of notes and complex panharmonic scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit complex panharmonic scales and many-stringed curiously-harmonised instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not maintain artisans who make complex multi-cornered lyres or instruments with panharmonic complexity; multiplicity of notes is unnecessary when only the Dorian and Phrygian are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The city will not support makers of overly complex stringed instruments; music is to be simple and martial in character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude flute and its panharmonic style from the city
rubrics_metrics.description: Flute-makers and flute-players are not admitted because the flute, in its composite use of harmony, is considered worse than the stringed instruments and a corrupting influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the lyre and the harp are permitted within the city; shepherds may have a pipe in the country, but the flute is rejected from the civic musical life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate rhythm to simple metres expressive of noble life
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythms (metres) should be simple and chosen to express the life of courage and order; avoid complex systems of metre and many kinds of rhythms that express meanness or insolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhythm and harmony should be regulated by the words (i.e., by the moral temper of the content). Socrates defers detailed technical classification to musical authorities (Damon) but insists on simplicity and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend censorship to visual and constructive arts (sculpture, building, crafts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control should not be limited to poets: sculptors, builders, weavers, embroiderers, and other artists must be prohibited from exhibiting vice, intemperance, meanness, and indecency in their works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists who cannot discern and represent the true nature of beauty and grace are to be prevented from practising, lest citizens' tastes be corrupted and youth grow up amid images of moral deformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical training as a primary formative instrument of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Music (rhythm and harmony) is a potent instrument because it fastens on the 'inward places of the soul' and imparts grace: right musical education makes the soul graceful; bad education makes it ungraceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-educated ear will perceive faults in art and nature and will early praise the good and hate the bad; hence musical instruction must be foundational and aligned with the moral curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians’ gymnastic training should produce resilient, wakeful bodies fit for campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: Gymnastic training should not produce the soft, sleepy bodies of ordinary athletes; rather it should make warrior-athletes who are wakeful, quick in senses, and resilient to changes of food and climate encountered on campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military gymnastic should be the 'twin sister' of the simple music prescribed. Avoid athletes' regimens that lead to vulnerability to illness if routine is disrupted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diet: favour simple soldiers’ fare, avoid sweet sauces and luxurious food
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians' food should be simple (soldiers' fare — roast rather than boiled, no sweet sauces) so they are not weakened by luxury and can endure campaigning conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homeric example: heroes on campaign eat simple fare. Sweet sauces and complex culinary indulgences are not mentioned approvingly in Homer and are to be avoided in the State's diet for guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstain from intoxication and prohibit drunkenness among guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must abstain from intoxication: a guardian should never be drunk or require another guardian to take care of him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drunkenness is incompatible with the wakeful, attentive responsibilities of guardians and is explicitly condemned as utterly unbecoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit sexual familiarity and forbid intemperate/unchaste expressions of love
rubrics_metrics.description: True love is temperate and a love of beauty and order; intemperate, sensual, or mad pleasures must be excluded from the relations of lovers. Familiarity should be limited to what a father uses to his son and only for noble purposes with consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law should regulate sexual familiarity so that excess and coarseness are judged guilty; mad or intemperate pleasure is to be kept away from lovers if their love is of the right sort.
